how-to-price-a-roof-by-the-square.html.text:
← Roofing bid calculator

How to price a roof by the square — not the house square footage

Homeowners and new crews search for “roofing cost calculator” and get a number times the house square footage. That is the floor plan. Roofers bid squares: 100 square feet of roof surface. The two numbers are not the same job.

A 1,800 sq ft ranch on a 6/12 pitch is about 20.1 squares of surface (1,800 × 1.118 ÷ 100), not 18. Add 10% waste for cuts, starter, and ridge and you are buying closer to 22.1 squares of covering. A 12/12 on the same footprint is about 25.5 squares before waste — forty percent more material and a slower, steeper crew day.

Tear-off is a second multiplier. One layer coming off is one pass of dump and labor on the existing surface. Two layers is twice the dump and twice the tear-off hours, on the same house. A flat “price per house square foot” cannot see any of that, which is how a bid that looked fine on a low-slope one-layer ranch loses money on a cut-up two-layer 10/12.

The roofing bid calculator does the arithmetic the trade already uses: footprint × pitch factor → squares, plus waste, layers, dump, loaded wage, overhead, and the margin you mean to keep. It also reports price per square and the walk-away number so you can score a cheaper quote against the same cost base.

Pitch factor is √(1 + (rise/12)²). Labor on 7/12–9/12 starts 25% slower, 10/12–12/12 50% slower, steeper than 12/12 twice as slow. Those steps are starting points, not a safety rating or a code opinion. Replace every default with your invoice and a rate timed from your crew.

Common questions

What is a roofing square?

A roofing square is 100 square feet of roof surface. It is not 100 square feet of the house floor plan.

Why is house square footage the wrong unit for a reroof bid?

Pitch turns footprint into more surface. A 6/12 roof is about 12% larger than its footprint; a 12/12 roof is about 41% larger. Waste and tear-off layers add more.

No warranty. This is not engineering, code, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell anyone what to charge. Verify measurements and costs before bidding.

FOR RESIDENTIAL ROOFING CONTRACTORS

Bid the roof, not the floor plan.

Price a reroof the way the trade actually does: each section’s footprint converted to roof squares by its pitch, plus waste, tear-off layers, dump, loaded labor, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the job price, what it works out to per square, and the number below which the job loses money. Why house square footage is the wrong unit · vs. a flat price per house square foot · This calculator vs. AccuLynx · vs. Jobber.

The roof

One row per section. Footprint is the area on the ground, not the shingle surface — pitch turns it into squares. Tear-off layers is how many existing roofs come off (0 for a new deck).

Where the labor goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting material and labor rates are common ballpark figures, not a supplier quote, a benchmark, or a guarantee — replace them with your invoice and your crew.

    Common questions

    How do I turn a house's square footage into roofing squares?

    You cannot, directly — that is the mistake this tool exists to stop. Enter each section's footprint (the area it covers on the ground) and its pitch, and the calculator multiplies the footprint by √(1 + (rise ÷ 12)²) to get actual roof surface, then divides by 100 to get squares. A 1,800 sq ft footprint at 6/12 is about 20 squares of roof, not 18. At 12/12 it is over 25. Bidding the footprint number buys you roughly one square of material short for every eight you ordered.

    Why does pitch change the price twice?

    Because it changes two different things. Steeper pitch means more surface for the same footprint, which is a material and a labor quantity. It also means slower, harder work on that surface, which is a labor rate. The second effect is the steepness multiplier: 1.0 up to 6/12, 1.25 through 9/12, 1.5 through 12/12, and 2.0 above that, applied to install and tear-off hours. Those steps are common shop starting points, not OSHA categories or a safety determination — a 12/12 walk-and- stage decision is yours, not the calculator's.

    Does waste apply to the tear-off as well as the new roof?

    No, and that is deliberate. Waste covers cuts, starter, ridge, and valleys on the new covering, so it is added only to the material squares that underlayment and covering are priced from. Tear-off follows the existing surface multiplied by how many layers are actually coming off, and dump cost follows those tear-off squares. A two-layer strip on a section is twice the tear-off and twice the landfill, but it does not double the shingles.

    Why price the garage and the porch as separate sections?

    Because they are usually a different pitch and a different number of existing layers, and a blended rate cannot see that. A steep detached garage or a porch cover carrying three layers is priced at its own pitch factor, its own steepness multiplier, and its own tear-off squares. One averaged "roof" row quietly moves cost from the hard section onto the easy one and leaves the bid short by whatever the hard section actually is.

    Why isn't a 20% margin the same as adding 20% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price, which is how the customer's number is quoted and how your P&L reads it: price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin). Overhead, separately, is a markup on the direct cost of the job — office, sales, and the insurance that is not already in payroll burden — and it is applied before margin, never to itself or to the profit. Marking a $10,000 cost up by 20% gives $12,000 and a 16.7% margin. Targeting a 20% margin gives $12,500. That gap is the whole job's profit on a small reroof.

    How much more does a metal roof cost than asphalt shingles?

    More than the material line alone shows. The covering presets here start 3-tab asphalt at $95 a square and architectural asphalt (this calculator's default) at $140, but standing-seam metal starts at $480 a square — a bit over three times the architectural material cost, and stone-coated steel and concrete tile sit in between at $360 and $420. Install labor climbs with it: 1.5 hours a square for 3-tab, 1.8 for architectural, up to 3.5 for standing-seam metal, because seaming and flashing panel roofing takes longer per square than nailing a shingle course. Picking a covering in the calculator fills material, underlayment, and install hours together, so the price gap you see includes both the pricier material and the slower crew day, not material cost by itself.

    Is my bid data uploaded anywhere?

    No. There is no account and no network request — every figure stays in this browser, including the business details saved for the printed proposal, which "Forget my business details" clears. "Copy share link" encodes the sections, rates, and deposit terms into the page's own URL hash so a partner or office can open the same bid; nothing is sent to a server. The optional local usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your roof measurements, wages, costs, or prices, and the checkbox in the footer turns it off.

    No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, engineering, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a structural, code, or safety determination. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, supplier invoices, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

    Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and never include your roof, wages, costs, or prices. A share link encodes only the quote fields in the page hash; it is not sent to us.

    Wrapping the walls on the same job? The siding bid calculator prices the net wall, the waste, the height, the openings, and the linear trim — nothing uploaded.

vs-a-flat-price-per-house-square-foot.ht.text:
← Roofing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat price per house square foot

“$7 a square foot, done” is not a price for a reroof — it is a price for one pitch and one tear-off layer, quietly applied to every house that calls in with a different footprint.

What a flat price per house square foot is

A flat price per house square foot is the fastest way to quote a reroof over the phone: multiply the house's footprint square footage by a number and read it back. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's quote will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of roof — usually a simple, low-slope main with one covering layer to tear off — and then reused for every house afterward, whether or not the next one is steep, carries a second or third layer underneath, or adds a garage, porch, or dormer at a different pitch.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each section's footprint and pitch, how many layers are coming off, waste, a material preset, install and tear-off hours, and your own wage, payroll burden, dump, permit, overhead, and target margin. It converts each section's footprint to actual roof surface using its pitch, prices material and labor by the square with a steep-labor multiplier, prices tear-off by the layer, and returns the job price, the price per square, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price — for this roof and this pitch, not a flat number for every house.

What a flat price per house square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee whether a section is a flat 4/12 or a steep 12/12, even though the steeper section has 41% more actual roof surface on the identical footprint. Converts each section's footprint to surface area with its own pitch factor (surface = footprint × √(1 + (rise/12)²)), then prices material and covers-per-square from the real surface, not the footprint.
Has no line for how steep a crew has to work — a 12/12 tear-off and install gets the same labor rate as a 4/12. Applies a steep-labor multiplier by pitch (up to double the normal rate above a 12/12) to both install and tear-off hours, so a harder-to-walk roof costs more to crew.
Quotes the same number for a single-layer tear-off and a two- or three-layer tear-off, with no separate line for the extra strip-off and dump. Prices tear-off surface as squares × layers, so a house with two layers of old shingles tears off, dumps, and bills for twice the material a single-layer house does.
Has no per-section breakdown — a steep garage or dormer eating a third of the labor on a fraction of the footprint disappears into one house-wide number. Prices every section — main, garage, porch, dormer, addition — on its own footprint, pitch, and tear-off layers, and reports each section's share of total labor hours.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the price per square, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two 2,200 sq ft footprints, one flat price

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

A 2,200 sq ft footprint — a 1,800 sq ft main house at a 6/12 pitch and a 400 sq ft attached garage at 4/12, both a single-layer tear-off — prices at $13,857.34 — $6.30 per footprint square foot — on a job that costs $11,085.87 to run.

Take the identical 2,200 sq ft footprint and make it a steeper roof instead — the main house at a 12/12 pitch and the garage at 10/12, both with a two-layer tear-off coming off first — and the job costs $19,652.96 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $24,566.20: $11.17 per footprint square foot, 1.77 times the easy job's price, on the identical footprint. Quoting the steep job at the easy job's flat $13,857.34 price prices it $5,795.62 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $10,708.86 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 20% target margin. Same footprint, same flat price, one roof that pays and one that loses money the moment the pitch and the tear-off layers show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per house square foot get a reroof wrong?

Because the cost driver is the roof's actual surface area and how many layers are coming off, not the house's footprint. A 1,800 sq ft main house at a 6/12 pitch has about 20.1 squares of roof surface, not 18; the same footprint at 12/12 has about 25.5 squares -- 41% more material and cutting for the identical footprint. Add a second tear-off layer and the crew is stripping twice the material before a single shingle goes down. A flat price per house square foot charges by the footprint because that is the only number it has, not because the footprint is what the job actually costs.

What does a flat price per house square foot usually leave out entirely?

Pitch and tear-off layers. A flat price has no line for a steep section's extra roof surface from the pitch factor, no line for the steep-labor multiplier a crew working a 12/12 actually needs versus a 6/12, and no separate line for a second or third tear-off layer, which doubles or triples the tear-off hours and dump weight on the same footprint. It also has no line that separates a low, simple main from a steep, multi-layer garage or dormer, since the flat number was set on the house's total footprint alone.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: a 2,200 sq ft footprint -- a 1,800 sq ft main at a 6/12 pitch and a 400 sq ft attached garage at 4/12, both single-layer tear-off -- prices at $13,857.34, on a job that costs $11,085.87 to run: $6.30 per footprint square foot. Take the identical 2,200 sq ft footprint and make the main 12/12 and the garage 10/12, both with a two-layer tear-off, and the job costs $19,652.96 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $24,566.20 -- $11.17 per footprint square foot, 1.77 times the easy job's price, on the identical footprint. Quoting the steep job at the easy job's flat $13,857.34 price prices it $5,795.62 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $10,708.86 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 20% target margin. Same footprint, same flat price, one roof that pays and one that loses money the moment the pitch and the tear-off layers show up.

Is a flat price per house square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar jobs -- a low-slope house with a single covering layer to tear off and no unusual sections -- a flat per-footprint-square-foot number can land close, because that is probably the job the price was set on. The risk is quoting a steep pitch, multiple tear-off layers, or a mix of sections (a main, a garage, a porch, a dormer) sight unseen, because the price does not know the pitch or the layer count until someone measures the roof, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market, your supplier's pricing, or your material costs. It takes each section's footprint, pitch, and tear-off layers, a material preset, waste, install and tear-off hours, your own wage, burden, dump, permit, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this roof -- the arithmetic a flat price per house square foot skips, not a market survey.

This calculator vs. AccuLynx

Two different shapes: AccuLynx is an account-based platform for running a roofing company's whole sales-to-production pipeline. This page is a free, private, no-account worksheet for one number — whether the price for one reroof, priced correctly by squares and pitch, actually clears your cost and margin.

What each tool is for

AccuLynx is a cloud-based business management platform built specifically for roofing contractors — it is not a generic construction or field-service tool. It is built around running a roofing company's whole pipeline in one account: lead capture and CRM, aerial roof measurement, estimating and proposal generation, material ordering with supplier integrations, production and crew scheduling, and job costing, used by a sales team, a production manager, and office staff together across every job the company runs, on an ongoing subscription. AccuLynx's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not track a lead, order material, schedule a crew, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one reroof — each section's footprint and pitch converted to actual roof squares, waste, how many layers are being torn off, a material preset, loaded labor, dump and permit, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns that into the job price, the price per square, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

They do different jobs. It takes one reroof's section footprints, pitch, waste, tear-off layers, material, loaded labor, dump, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price per square, an effective hourly rate, and a walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal, instantly, in the browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A roofing company running leads, crews, and material orders across many jobs at once is better served by AccuLynx or a comparable platform; a contractor who wants an instant, private, correctly-pitched price for one roof before a bid goes out is in the right place here.
